results.name: Required sections present
results.criterion: The lesson has an H2 section for each of: what is RAG, why it matters, how it works, a worked example, limits, recap, a self-check quiz, and key words.

results.name: Short sentences
results.criterion: Average sentence length <= 15 words AND no sentence longer than 25 words.
evidence: (43 words) First, it only knows what was in its training data (the past books and text the AI read to learn) up to a cutoff date (a knowledge cutoff, which is the date after which the AI has no new information in its memory).
results.fix: Split every sentence longer than 25 words into two or three short sentences. One idea per sentence.

results.name: Plain-English readability
results.criterion: Flesch Reading Ease >= 60 on the lesson prose.

results.name: Right length for one sitting
results.criterion: Between 700 and 1800 words (~10-15 minutes of reading for a slow reader).

results.name: Self-check with answers
results.criterion: The quiz section has at least 3 questions and gives the answers.

results.name: No false or misleading claims
results.criterion: Every technical claim agrees with the reference facts. No listed misconception is stated or implied as true. Simplifications are allowed only if they do not create a wrong belief (e.g. 'the model learns your documents' is a FAIL, because RAG does not change the model).
results.reasoning: I checked all the accuracy requirements against the lesson text and found no misconceptions, false claims, or prohibited implications. Every technical claim aligns precisely with the reference facts provided.

results.name: All must-cover points taught
results.criterion: Every must-cover point in the reference is actually taught (explained, not just named).
results.reasoning: I checked every single must-cover item (M1 through M9) against the lesson text. All nine points are clearly explained, well-structured, and easy to understand for the target beginner audience.

results.name: Every technical term explained
results.criterion: Every technical or English-uncommon term is explained in simple words at or before its first use in the body (a glossary at the end alone does not count). Acronyms are expanded on first use.
results.reasoning: I checked every technical and uncommon term in the lesson against the requirement. Every single term including AI model, LLM, prompt, retrieval, embedding, chunk, hallucination, and weights is clearly explained in simple words at or before its first appearance in the body text.

results.name: Concrete analogy and walk-through
results.criterion: The lesson has (a) at least one everyday analogy a young Indian learner would recognise, correctly mapped to RAG, AND (b) one concrete worked example that follows a single question through every step: preparing documents, retrieving, adding to the prompt, generating.
results.reasoning: I checked the lesson for an everyday analogy (open-book exam) that a young Indian learner would recognize and verified that it maps correctly to RAG. I also checked the worked example section to ensure it clearly traces a single question through document preparation, retrieval, prompt augmentation, and generation.

results.name: Fits a non-native English beginner
results.criterion: Uses common, everyday English words; no idioms, slang, sarcasm or culturally obscure references; assumes no coding, maths beyond class 12, or prior AI knowledge; tone is encouraging and direct.
results.reasoning: The lesson uses simple, straightforward English that is completely appropriate for a non-native beginner. It avoids idioms, slang, and complex grammatical structures while addressing the learner directly with a warm tone. No prior knowledge of coding or advanced mathematics is assumed or required.

results.name: Builds step by step
results.criterion: Ideas are introduced before they are used; sections go from what -> why -> how -> example -> limits -> recap; each section links to the previous one; nothing is repeated without purpose.
results.reasoning: The lesson follows the exact required section order from what you will learn down to key words. Each technical term and concept is introduced clearly before being referenced later. Transitions between sections are smooth, creating a logical flow from LLM basics to RAG definition, mechanics, examples, limits, and review. Analogies are appropriately placed and discussed.

change_log.change: Removed the false paragraph claiming RAG retrains the AI model and ensures always-correct answers.
Removed the contradictory false teaching that RAG retrains models and guarantees correctness.
Added simple explanations for training data, cutoff date, knowledge cutoff, and weights at their first use.
Removed the incorrect introductory sentence about retraining in the RAG section so ideas flow logically without contradiction.
